title: 1 Samuel 6:19–21
context: The joy of the ark’s return is met by judgment. The LORD struck men of Beth Shemesh, because they had looked into the LORD’s ark; the WEB says he struck “fifty thousand seventy” of the men, and the people mourned, because the LORD had struck the people with a great slaughter. The men of Beth Shemesh ask who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God, and to whom he shall go up from them. They send messengers to Kiriath Jearim to say that the Philistines have brought back the LORD’s ark, and to ask those inhabitants to come down and bring it up to themselves. Both traditions take the scene as a confession of the LORD’s holiness after irreverence toward the ark. Two well-known difficulties should be handled as open questions, not as consensus and not as an Arminian–Reformed contrast. First, the number in verse 19 is a famous text-critical issue: the WEB, with the Masoretic wording, has the large figure “fifty thousand seventy”, and some witnesses and translations read seventy; this eBible page carries no footnote on the verse, and the printed WEB text is the large number. Second, WEB’s “looked into” the ark is sometimes rendered as looking at or upon it; the exact force of the looking is discussed, but both traditions agree that the offense is irreverence toward what is holy.

verses.text: He struck of the men of Beth Shemesh, because they had looked into the LORD’s ark, he struck fifty thousand seventy of the men. Then the people mourned, because the LORD had struck the people with a great slaughter.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He struck of the men of Beth Shemesh, because they had looked into the LORD’s ark, he struck fifty thousand seventy of the men.” Then the people mourned, because the LORD had struck the people with “a great slaughter.”

Arminian readers take the judgment as real and as tied to an irreverent looking. WEB says they “looked into the LORD’s ark”; some translations speak of looking at or upon it, and the precise force of the verb is a known question, not a point on which the two traditions divide. The large number “fifty thousand seventy” is likewise a famous text-critical issue. Some witnesses and translations read seventy. This eBible chapter has no footnote here; the WEB text we follow is the large number, and neither figure should be declared the settled original by a guess in a note.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise stress that it is the LORD who struck, and that the people mourn a great slaughter. The cause named in this wording is that they had looked into the ark: a failure of reverence after the joy of verse 13 and the offerings of verses 14–15. Whether “looked into” means prying inside or an irreverent looking at or upon the ark remains debated; both readings still leave the offense as unholy curiosity or disregard.

The number is a known problem, not a party contrast. The WEB, with the Masoretic tradition’s large figure, reads “fifty thousand seventy”; some witnesses and translations read seventy. A total so large has long seemed hard for a single town, which is one reason the smaller reading is discussed. The notes cannot settle the manuscripts, and they should not invent a list of witnesses beyond that general, well-known fact.

verses.text: The men of Beth Shemesh said, “Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? To whom shall he go up from us?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The men of Beth Shemesh said, “Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? To whom shall he go up from us?” The slaughter is answered by a confession and by a question about where the ark should go.

Arminian readers hear a right fear after a real judgment. They name the LORD “this holy God”, and they ask who can stand before him. The holiness is not an abstraction; it has just been felt, and the question of a resting place is serious.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same two questions: who can stand, and to whom shall he go up. The LORD is confessed as holy, and Beth Shemesh does not assume that the ark is now theirs to treat as they please.

Both traditions take the verse as shared ground in the holiness of God. The fear is fitting; the next verse will send for another town to come and take the ark up.

verses.text: They sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath Jearim, saying, “The Philistines have brought back the LORD’s ark. Come down and bring it up to yourselves.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath Jearim, saying, “The Philistines have brought back the LORD’s ark. Come down and bring it up to yourselves.” The ark is offered to another Israelite town, named as the WEB spells it, Kiriath Jearim.

Arminian readers hear a real handing-on. Beth Shemesh does not keep the ark after this blow; they ask Kiriath Jearim to come down and bring it up, and chapter 7 will show that request received.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the message as the outworking of verse 20. The ark is still the LORD’s; it is not abandoned, but it is sent to people who will be asked to house it.

Both traditions read the verse as the link into the next chapter, shared narrative ground, without a contrast over why Kiriath Jearim is chosen. The text itself does not say.
